extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of English literature / literary criticism
extracted.subtask_description: Lecture-style critical criteria for evaluating English poets, poetic genres (pastoral, descriptive, fable), and prose style — with examples and standards drawn from canonical authors. Focused on what makes poetic description, pastoral, fable, and prose effective or defective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Still-life of tragedy (Crabbe)
rubrics_metrics.description: A poet may attempt the 'still life of tragedy' — giving stagnation of hope and fear, the deformity of vice without temptation, the pain of sympathy without interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This approach relies on truth and accuracy in describing only what is disagreeable; it tends to convey little delight because it depicts misery and helplessness without generating sympathetic involvement or dramatic tension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Descriptive poetry — source of excellence
rubrics_metrics.description: The best descriptive poetry is not necessarily written by the self-styled descriptive poets (examples: Milton's Lycidas and The Winter's Tale surpass set descriptions in Thomson, Cowper, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High-quality description combines imaginative power and appropriateness to subject rather than mere cataloguing of natural objects; look to unexpected sources (dramatic or epic poetry) for superior descriptive passages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pastoral authenticity
rubrics_metrics.description: True pastorals require suitability of manners and atmosphere (Arcadian manners, a fitting climate, simplicity of life); England lacks an eternal-spring Arcadia, so our pastorals differ from Theocritus or Claude Lorraine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective pastoral writing evokes the simplicity, healthy employments, piety, and humane feeling appropriate to rural life (example praised: Walton's Complete Angler for simplicity and romantic interest). Avoid incongruous Arcadian artifices unsuited to local realities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity and humanity in pastoral/prose-poem
rubrics_metrics.description: Walton's Complete Angler exemplifies a pastoral prose-poem with beauty and romantic interest arising from simplicity and the author's piety and humanity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Descriptions of ordinary things (a fishing-tackle, an inn meal) should reveal the author's humane sensibility; good pastoral values 'good cheer' and everyday realities as sources of poetic feeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Association and abstractedness in nature-writing
rubrics_metrics.description: The distinctive source of our love of country is its abstractedness: interest in natural objects is common and transferable across a class of objects, rooted in association of ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective nature-writing ties physical objects to habitual associations (childhood, solitude, memories) so that small familiar images evoke deep feeling and a transferable, universal sentiment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evoking strong emotions through insignificant objects
rubrics_metrics.description: Insignificant and rudest objects often connect with the strongest emotions because they are habitually associated with personal recollections and feelings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writers should use common, familiar images (a post, a little spot of green, a daisy) that function like old acquaintances to trigger deep emotional responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universality and consistency of natural imagery
rubrics_metrics.description: Nature presents a 'universal home' whose objects remain essentially the same across seasons; the consistent, recurring aspects of nature give comfort and continuity to feeling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good nature-writing emphasizes recurring, recognizable images (sun, moon, trees in different seasons) to produce a 'mystic personification' and an undivided spirit across scenes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prose-style terseness and conciseness (Arbuthnot)
rubrics_metrics.description: A high prose style is distinguished by terseness: leaving out superfluous words, sparing connecting particles and introductory phrases, and using the simplest constructions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for economy of expression and precise phrasing; avoid needless ornaments that obscure meaning. Mastery includes knowing which plain English word exactly matches the intended idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Word-choice precision and idiomatic mastery
rubrics_metrics.description: Each common English word carries different associations and shades of meaning; perfection of conversational prose is having all these at command and choosing the exact word called for by the occasion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate fine discrimination between near-synonyms; prefer the familiar word that fits the idea rather than learned or foreign substitutes lacking nuance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variety and adaptation in prose
rubrics_metrics.description: A good modern prose style should have variety of inflection and adaptation to the subject; lack of such variety makes the style hinder perception of differences between things described.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid monotonous learned diction; vary sentence forms and register to suit different subjects and preserve clarity and discrimination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opposition to florid learned style
rubrics_metrics.description: Florid or artificial styles (scalped from foreign languages) substitute learned words for the nuanced native words and thus lose the finer inflections of meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious about adopting pompous Latinate or foreign-sounding words that are not idiomatic; they may impress but obscure precision and subtlety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Johnsonian Latinate jargon (critique)
rubrics_metrics.description: Dr. Johnson's habit of taking the first English word and translating it into a Latin/Greek equivalent half-way produces a jargon which imposes generalization and confounds ranks in literature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware of manufactured 'learned' diction that substitutes length and foreignness for true expressive power; such jargon may spread into advertisements and popular prose with deleterious effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Naturalness of diction — writing as speech
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors of the Queen Anne age wrote as people spoke; contemporary affectation is to 'speak as authors write', which is criticized — retaining the mother tongue in writing or conversation is a virtue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strive for natural, conversational idiom in appropriate contexts; don't let artifice make written language alien from ordinary speech when clarity and intimacy are needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Playful indirectness and suggestiveness (Prior)
rubrics_metrics.description: Good light lyric or fugitive pieces may 'glance' at subjects with laughing grace, insinuate what cannot be directly insisted upon, half-concealing and half-revealing with archness and careless raillery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use indirect suggestion, ironic hinting, and playful omission to produce charm and wit; let the poem suggest more than it states outright.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticity vs sentimental affectation (Prior)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sentimental and romantic productions that result from conscious artifice rather than powerful impulse or real feeling are mere affectation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether emotional expression is genuine (impulsive, felt) or manufactured by labouring art; the latter weakens poetic authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy and point in fables
rubrics_metrics.description: A fable should combine invention with elegant, facile execution; faults include being spun out too long, diffuse descriptions, desultory narrative, and morals without point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep fables concise, focused, and pointed; ensure the moral or lesson is sharp and integral to the narrative rather than tacked-on or vague.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transformation of base materials into refined art (Beggar's Opera)
rubrics_metrics.description: A work can take vulgar or low materials and, by wit and artistry, extract an essence of refinement without violating probability or the modesty of nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Successful satire or comic-drama preserves authenticity of character while elevating language and thought, so low life is rendered with dignity, wit, and philosophical insight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preservation of character and costume
rubrics_metrics.description: Complete preservation of character and costume is crucial to the success of works depicting low life (as in the Beggar's Opera).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain fidelity to social types and realistic detail; costume and manner must be convincing to sustain the transformation and the satire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance of wit and moral sympathy in satire
rubrics_metrics.description: Wit can temper offensiveness of satire and humanize even high public figures; the best satire exposes vulgarity of vice while enabling readers (even powerful ones) to laugh at themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for satire that combines sharpness with humane understanding so that it instructs without alienating the audience entirely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral purpose should illuminate social commonality
rubrics_metrics.description: A successful moral in satire or comedy may show that the same violations of integrity and sophistry are common to both great and mean — exposing a universal vulgarity of vice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use moral insight to reveal common human failings across ranks rather than to punish a single class; make the lesson general and revealing.
